Evaluation Team ii F R ON T M AT T E R Disclaimer This report presents an independent impact evaluation of the Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM) investments in Nigeria. The evaluation was commissioned by the Global Fund through the Principal Recipients — the National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA), the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme (NTBLCP) and the Lagos State Ministry of Health. The evaluation was conducted by Jhpiego (Affiliate of Johns Hopkins University) as the technical evaluation partner. The findings, interpretations, conclusions and recommendations expressed in this report are those of the evaluation team. They do not necessarily represent the official positions of the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, the Government of Nigeria, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, NACA, NTBLCP, or any of the institutions that participated in the evaluation.

t: Disclaimer The report draws on data
x: Disclaimer The report draws on data collected from national, state and facility-level sources and on documentary records made available to the evaluation team. While reasonable measures were taken to verify and triangulate the information presented, the analysis reflects the data available at the time of fieldwork; investments that were ongoing at that time are identified as such, and conclusions concerning them are correspondingly qualified. All data are presented in deidentified form. Key informants are referred to by role and state, and no individual respondent can be identified from the contents of this report. iii F R ON T M AT T E R Foreword The COVID-19 pandemic represented one of the greatest tests of Nigeria's health system in recent history. It challenged institutions at every level and demanded a response that extended beyond traditional programme boundaries. What began as an urgent effort to save lives and contain transmission evolved into a broader national effort to strengthen systems, protect essential services, and improve preparedness for future public health threats.

t: The Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism
x: The Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM) provided Nigeria with an important financing window to pursue these objectives simultaneously. While supporting the immediate response to COVID-19, the investments increasingly shifted toward building resilient and sustainable systems for health. Resources initially directed to diagnostics, treatment, oxygen and infection prevention gradually expanded into strengthening laboratory networks, surveillance systems, emergency preparedness, supply chains, digital health platforms, the health workforce, and mechanisms to safeguard HIV, tuberculosis and malaria services. This report is therefore not only an evaluation of the emergency response, but also of how crisis-driven investments contributed to longer-term health system resilience. As Principal Recipient for the larger share of the C19RM portfolio, the National Agency for the Control of AIDS worked closely with the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme, federal and state institutions, Sub-Recipients, Technical Support Organisations, civil society organisations, development partners and the Country Coordinating Mechanism to implement this complex and evolving portfolio.

t: The achievements described in this report
x: The achievements described in this report are the product of this collective effort and of the commitment demonstrated by institutions and frontline workers across the country. This evaluation comes at an important moment. Nigeria is advancing the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and strengthening implementation of the National Action Plan for Health Security. Understanding which investments translated into durable capacities, which gains remain vulnerable, and what lessons should inform future investments is essential as the country moves toward greater domestic ownership and prepares for the next generation of health security challenges. I welcome the rigour and independence with which this evaluation was conducted. By combining internationally recognised evaluation criteria with a theory-based contribution analysis, the report provides a balanced assessment of what was achieved, the contextual factors that shaped implementation, and the areas where further action is required. Beyond accountability, it offers practical lessons for sustaining the capacities built through C19RM and for informing future investments under the Global Fund and other health security initiatives.

x: I wish to acknowledge the Global Fund for its continued partnership and support to Nigeria, the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme for its stewardship of key components of the portfolio, the Federal Ministry of Health, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency, state governments, implementing partners, civil society organisations and all those who contributed to the implementation of these investments. I also commend the evaluation team for undertaking this work with scientific rigour and professionalism. It is my hope that this report will serve not only as a record of what was accomplished during an unprecedented period, but also as a guide for sustaining these gains and strengthening Nigeria's preparedness for future public health emergencies. The main durable contribution of the response should not be the memory of the crisis itself, but the systems strengthened through the response. t: In Nigeria, responding to the crisis
x: In Nigeria, responding to the crisis required unprecedented collaboration across institutions, programmes and partners, while underscoring the need to maintain essential services even during periods of significant disruption. As a Principal Recipient of the Global Fund COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C19RM), the National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Control Programme (NTBLCP) was entrusted with key investments in Primary Health Care Revitalization, laboratory equipment, medical oxygen and respiratory care, health product supply chains — warehouse upgrades, and the continuity of tuberculosis and other essential services. Working closely with subrecipients, technical support organisations and stakeholders at national and sub-national levels, the Programme helped strengthen capacities whose value extends well beyond the immediate demands of the pandemic. These investments also supported longer-term system needs. Through the C19RM portfolio, we supported laboratory and diagnostic systems, the medical oxygen and respiratory-care ecosystem, health product warehousing and supply chain systems, and interventions designed to protect tuberculosis and other essential health services from disruption.

t: Many of these investments have become
x: Many of these investments have become enduring assets that continue to support routine service delivery and strengthen preparedness for future health threats. One of the clearest lessons from this experience is that investments in one part of the health system often generate benefits across many others. Strengthening diagnostics, oxygen infrastructure, supply chains and service continuity has reinforced capacities that support not only tuberculosis control, but also broader health security and emergency preparedness. These linked gains show the value of investing in resilient and sustainable systems and contribute to strengthening the core capacities required under the International Health Regulations. This evaluation comes at an important time as Nigeria advances the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative and implements the National Action Plan for Health Security. Beyond documenting achievements, the report provides important evidence on implementation experiences, persisting gaps and the actions required to sustain and build on the gains that have been made.

It is my hope that the evidence generated through this evaluation will help guide future investments and support the continued strengthening of Nigeria's health system and preparedness for emerging public health threats. t: C19RM was designed to support the
x: C19RM was designed to support the immediate COVID-19 response, protect HIV, tuberculosis and malaria services from disruption, and strengthen systems for future public-health emergencies. Having commenced with an emergency-response wave in 2020–2021, it transitioned to a fast-track scale-up wave in 2022–2024 and then a pandemic-preparedness wave through to 2026, with investment across the health system to scale up Nigeria’s capacity to prevent, detect and respond to outbreaks and public-health emergencies. The evaluation applied a theory-based, mixed-methods design using contribution analysis, assessing performance against the six OECD-DAC criteria, with Equity and System Risk as cross-cutting lenses and contribution claims tested against Mayne’s six standards. Prior to COVID-19, Nigeria’s ability to respond to a health emergency was its weakest area of readiness. On the 2017 Joint External Evaluation (JEE), the Respond pillar scored 33%, against a national average of 39%, and the core capacities an emergency response depends on sat at the bottom of the scale: there was no national emergencypreparedness plan in use, no system to send or receive medical supplies in a crisis, limited mechanisms for rapid health-worker deployment, and weak or underdeveloped health-security coordination mechanisms. By the 2019 midterm review the Respond score had risen to 46%, but important gaps remained. Nigeria therefore entered the pandemic with a system that was improving but not yet ready for a shock on this scale.

The module was delivered through the national Principal Recipients, NACA and NTBLCP, alongside complementary investment from USAID, CHAI, UNITAID, UNICEF and WHO. The oxygen scale-up was funded by several actors at once; C19RM is assessed throughout as one contributor among several rather than the sole cause of observed change.

Liquid-oxygen losses, and the engineering fixes that followed Liquid oxygen carried its own efficiency penalty and its own remedy. Cryogenic tanks continuously vent vaporised oxygen, so tanks with slow draw-off lose product; several tanks were also left unused for two to three years after installation because of safety gaps, delaying operationalisation; and hauling oxygen can cost upward of 30% of the oxygen itself. In the first phase (2020–21), coordination that had run on ad-hoc escalation was pulled into PHEOCs as the place where surveillance signals, laboratory information and response decisions could be organised. In the third phase (2024–26), the emergency-management workforce widened to 480 responders across 24 states and the FCT, event-based surveillance was routed into PHEOC workflows, and simulation exercises shifted the test of readiness from whether a plan existed to whether teams had practised activating, coordinating and standing down.

These are pre-and-post facility-monitoring figures from the supported facilities rather than a controlled outcome evaluation, so they are read as a contribution to service-delivery quality within QI sites, consistent with the maturity gains, and not as population-level impact. Quality Improvement is the clearest case of a capability C19RM catalysed through reprogramming rather than original design, and it illustrates the difference between financing an activity and scaling one. It was not part of the original C19RM design and had no dedicated budget line. It began under the Global Fund Service Delivery Innovation Strategic Initiative, delivered through the Resilient and Sustainable Systems for Health platform, as a pilot in five of Jigawa State’s local government areas, where Jhpiego provided technical assistance. Roughly US$2.8 million of C19RM resources, reprogrammed under the Global Fund’s flexibility to reprioritise during the response, with NACA as Principal Recipient and Jhpiego as Technical Support Organisation, then financed the scale-up: a new implementation in Ekiti and Gombe and extended coverage in Jigawa.

t: C19RM therefore catalysed the scale-up of
x: C19RM therefore catalysed the scale-up of an existing pilot, not the creation of Quality Improvement. The catalysed category is the smallest of the three but the one most directly linked to C19RM, because it was financed from within the grant through reprogramming and savings. The clearest documented example is Quality Improvement; a smaller instance was the reprogramming of risk-communication funds for additional social-media and infodemic-management activity. Both are set out below, and neither was part of the original C19RM design. t: The national digital-system costs, software licences,
x: The national digital-system costs, software licences, internet and IT support, are by far the most donor-dependent stream, with about four in five assessed sites reporting these still run on donor funds or nothing (donor-dependent 79%, 95% CI 60 to 91). By contrast, the physical infrastructure has largely transitioned to domestic funding: warehouse operations are 91% domestically financed, IPC consumables 83%, and oxygen-plant running costs 76%. Commodities and buildings are being absorbed by government and hospital revenue; the recurrent costs of platforms, connectivity and IT support are not. This reframes the sustainability finding that appears in every module’s system-risk section. The risk is not a flat, portfolio-wide absence of domestic budget; it is a specific donor-dependence in the digital, data-platform and connectivity recurrent costs. The implication is a targeted one: domestic budget lines should be ring-fenced first for the recurrent software, connectivity and IT-support costs of the data and surveillance platforms, which are the streams least likely to continue after donor exit, rather than a blanket call to domesticate all recurrent costs.

It not only protected the essential programs of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria, but It extended the value of emergency investments into routine health care and future preparedness. The Global Fund's COVID-19 Response Mechanism supported Nigeria in managing an extraordinary public health emergency while strengthening the systems required for future outbreaks and pandemic preparedness. Implemented from April 2021 to December 2025 through key government institutions, Principal Recipients, Sub-recipients, technical partners, states, facilities and communities, the portfolio reached all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. Its contribution extended beyond the immediate pandemic of the COVID19 response to expand the reach, depth and strengthen the landscape of Surveillance, laboratory systems, medical oxygen ecosystem, infection prevention and control systems, emergency coordination response, supply chains and warehousing sub-nationally, responsive digital platforms, workforce development and community systems translating to a robust national and subnational health security infrastructure.

The Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL) was transformed into a National Genomics and Bioinformatics Centre through major infrastructure upgrades and installation of high-throughput sequencing platforms, multi-omics technologies, highperformance computing (HPC) clusters, and supporting information technology infrastructure, significantly strengthening Nigeria's capacity for genomic surveillance, bioinformatics analysis, and advanced public health laboratory research.

t: A national genomic sequencing strategy was
x: A national genomic sequencing strategy was taken from a blank page to a ministerial launch in under eighteen months — a zero draft at a Lagos stakeholder event in May 2024, a validation workshop in Abuja in July 2024, and a national launch under the Coordinating Minister for Health in October 2024. The National Genomic Surveillance Consortium was inaugurated by the NCDC Director-General to provide permanent coordination. The strategy defined priority pathogens, coverage targets, data-ownership and sharing rules, institutional roles and the reporting pathway from sequencing result to surveillance action before sequencing scaled. Genomic data now flow into national surveillance structures, and the capability extends well beyond COVID-19 to Lassa virus, mpox, cholera, diphtheria and antimicrobial resistance. The forward task is to hold and widen that gain — financing reagents domestically, keeping the consortium active, and expanding pathogen coverage, the analytical workforce and the number of sequencing nodes.

t: Nigeria’s C19RM surveillance investments addressed a
x: Nigeria’s C19RM surveillance investments addressed a core health-security problem exposed by COVID-19: the country’s surveillance system had national structures, but functionality was uneven across states, LGAs, facilities and communities. Delays in case detection, paper-based workflows, limited digital reporting points, weak community signal capture, uneven IDSR capacity, and interoperability reduced the speed at which public health threats could be detected, verified, escalated, and acted upon. C19RM supported a layered surveillance-strengthening approach rather than a single-platform intervention. SORMAS, Nigeria’s national disease surveillance and outbreak management platform operated by NCDC for case/event-based reporting, case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory linkage and outbreak coordination, was deployed nationally. By September 2020, it had reached all 774 LGAs, but only 155 health facilities, 15 treatment centres, 26 laboratories and 25 points of entry.

t: The C19RM investment expanded SORMAS use
x: The C19RM investment expanded SORMAS use across tertiary, secondary and selected primary health-care facilities in all 36 states and the FCT; trained users to support electronic reporting, case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory linkage and outbreak coordination; strengthened IDSR capacity among frontline health workers and surveillance personnel; decentralised Event-Based Surveillance to 12 states; piloted Community-Based Surveillance in 63 LGAs across Kano, Oyo and Enugu; and introduced the 7-1-7 framework as a practical benchmark for reviewing outbreak detection, notification and early response. The evidence presented shows important system-strengthening outputs: 5,084 SORMAS users trained, 3,720 facilities supported, 5,700 devices distributed, over 40,000 health workers trained in IDSR, 360 multisectoral EBS participants trained across 12 states, and 6,930 community informants trained under CBS pilots. Reporting completeness reportedly improved from 71% to 93%, and timeliness from 64% to 85% on SORMAS post-training.

t: The most significant contribution of the
x: The most significant contribution of the surveillance investment was the shift from a facility-heavy, largely paper-dependent surveillance model to a more layered early-warning system that links facilities, LGAs, states, community informants, event-based intelligence, and emergency-response structures. This represents a credible contribution to Nigeria’s IHR and JEE surveillance priorities, particularly in digital reporting, early warning, event verification, community-based surveillance, and response coordination. However, the system is not yet fully mature. SORMAS-DHIS2 interoperability remains incomplete; private-sector reporting is not yet systematically institutionalised; EBS and CBS remain partial rather than fully established national functions; device maintenance, data support, and workforce turnover remain risks; and One Health information-sharing across the human, animal, and environmental sectors requires clearer governance. t: PHASE 2 PHASE 3 Emergency Surveillance
x: PHASE 2 PHASE 3 Emergency Surveillance Response. The first phase revealed how unevenly the system performed under pressure. Local-government capacity varied widely; facility detection was constrained by limited training, competing clinical workloads and paper-based workflows; and community reporting was weakest in the very places where public health events often emerge first - rural and hard-to-reach areas. Although electronic reporting is part of the revised IDSR, the phased rollout of SORMAS remains incomplete, particularly in secondary and tertiary facilities, limiting real-time reporting and data visibility. IDSR training had not yet been completed in health facilities across all states, leaving implementation uneven and adherence to the revised guidelines variable. EBS existed at the national level, but functional EBS structures were not yet established at the intermediate level, reducing the ability to detect outbreaks early through community and event signals.

x: This phase clarified the core problem: Nigeria needed a surveillance system that was not only national but also functional at the state, LGA, facility and community levels. Building the Digital Surveillance System. The scale-up phase built that functionality. SORMAS was deployed across all 36 states and the FCT, with a focus on secondary, tertiary and selected primary health facilities. This strengthened electronic notification, case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory data management and outbreak coordination. Thousands of surveillance officers, clinicians, laboratory personnel and facility focal persons were trained to use the platform, and digital devices were distributed to support field reporting. IDSR training was conducted in the remaining 20 states not covered by the previous World Bank REDISSE II grant, translating updated guidance into routine practice across a workforce affected by transfers and attrition. Event-Based Surveillance was operationalised in 12 states, bringing epidemic intelligence closer to where signals first appear.

The 7-1-7 framework gave surveillance and response teams a clear discipline and a practical way to measure the speed of outbreak management. Reporting completeness and timeliness both improved markedly over the period. Early work also began on interoperability between SORMAS and the routine health information system, DHIS2, as a first step toward a harmonised digital system in which surveillance, laboratory and routine data connect. Early engagement with private-sector reporting also emerged as a priority, although interoperability remained incomplete. The surveillance investments were also linked to the wider emergency-operations scale-up, giving surveillance signals a coordinated response home, as detailed in the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response chapter. t: Before the investment, many community-level signals
x: Before the investment, many community-level signals were likely to enter the surveillance system only after affected persons presented at a health facility or after an unusual event had already attracted wider attention. This was a particular concern in rural, underserved, hard-to-reach and high-mobility settings, where unusual illnesses, deaths, rumours or clusters may spread before they are formally notified. The CBS pilots in Kano, Oyo and Enugu responded to this gap by training 6,930 community informants across 63 LGAs to identify and report unusual illnesses, unexplained deaths, rumours and priority-disease signals. This shift is important because early warning does not depend only on health-facility data. Signals may first appear in households, markets, schools, religious gatherings, farms, transport hubs, border communities or other local settings where people notice abnormal patterns before the formal health system has sufficient routine data.

t: Community-Based Surveillance, therefore, provides a bridge
x: Community-Based Surveillance, therefore, provides a bridge between local observations and public health action, especially when community informants are trusted, supervised, linked to DSNOs or other designated surveillance officers, and given feedback on reported alerts. Event-Based Surveillance added another layer to this early-warning model. Through EBS operationalisation in 12 states, state teams were provided with structures to identify, triage, verify, and escalate signals from the media, hotlines, community reports, and other informal or non-routine sources recognised in EBS protocols. This complemented indicator-based surveillance, which remains the backbone for structured reporting of suspected and confirmed priority diseases through established health-facility and public health reporting channels. SORMAS strengthened the facility and subnational digital reporting pathway by supporting electronic notification, case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory linkage and outbreak coordination.

t: IDSR training aimed to improve the
x: IDSR training aimed to improve the ability of frontline workers, surveillance focal persons and DSNOs to apply standard case definitions, report priority diseases, recognise thresholds, document events and escalate public health signals. Together, SORMAS, IDSR capacity-building, EBS and CBS expanded Nigeria’s early-warning reach by increasing the number and diversity of signal sources available to the surveillance system. A major contribution of the surveillance pillar was the movement from a predominantly facility-based reporting model toward a more layered early-warning system. The investment strengthened complementary surveillance functions: indicator-based surveillance through routine facility reporting and SORMAS-enabled notification; event-based surveillance through state-level signal detection, triage, verification and escalation; and community-based surveillance through trained community informants who could report unusual events before they entered formal health-care channels.

Across the project lifecycle, the operational core of the RCCE framework demonstrated that interventions work best when they are heavily localised, directly linked to trusted community actors, and integrated with service-continuity and NPI promotion. t: Despite strong delivery, the CSS intervention
x: Despite strong delivery, the CSS intervention faced clear operational and sustainability risks. These challenges affected the speed, continuity and institutionalisation of community-led monitoring. They also sharpened one of the intervention’s most important lessons: CSS proved its value through the scale of issues identified, advocacy conducted and issues resolved, but that value will only last if the model is financed, protected and absorbed into routine health system accountability. Payment Delays Payment delays were a major constraint. Late disbursements from the Principal Recipient delayed monthly allowances to community monitoring teams, slowed early start-up and affected community trust. This mattered because CSS depended on active field presence. Across the portfolio, community structures identified 12,130 issues, conducted 16,362 advocacy visits and resolved 5,856 issues. Delays therefore had direct implications for follow-up, verification, escalation and issue resolution. When community teams are not supported on time, the accountability chain weakens.

t: Donor Dependency A second blind spot
x: Donor Dependency A second blind spot was sustainability financing. Community-led monitoring still depends heavily on donor funding, while state and local health departments do not yet have dedicated budget lines for CLM activities, supervision, transport, data validation or advocacy follow-up. This creates a real risk for the unresolved backlog of approximately 6,274 issues, which still requires continued escalation and system response. Without domestic financing, CLM risks remaining a project activity rather than a routine PHC accountability mechanism. Insecurity and Rising Field Costs Security concerns also affected implementation. Insecurity in some communities disrupted movement, field activities and timelines, limiting the ability of CLMTs and CBOs to maintain regular contact with facilities and communities. Inflation worsened this constraint. Persistent increases in transport costs and other logistics expenses reduced field reach, especially in hard-to-reach locations where community monitoring is often most needed. Together, insecurity and inflation increased the cost of accountability.

t: Withdrawal of Partner Support The withdrawal
x: Withdrawal of Partner Support The withdrawal of support from some partner organisations also affected activities that relied on their platforms, logistics or community structures. This exposed a wider continuity risk. Where CSS activities depend too heavily on temporary partner support, implementation can weaken once those partners reduce involvement or shift priorities. The model therefore needs stronger continuity planning, clearer ownership and a transition pathway that does not rely only on external partner systems. Bureaucracy Government bureaucracy created further delays. Advocacy engagements were sometimes slowed by approval processes, delayed responses and late redemption of government commitments. This weakened the accountability loop. Issues could be identified, evidence could be presented and commitments could be secured, but action was not always timely. For CLM to work as intended, government response must be predictable, documented and time-bound. Ownership Finally, the lack of dedicated budgets for state actors limited ownership.

t: Without financing for state coordination, supervision,
x: Without financing for state coordination, supervision, review meetings, data use and follow-up advocacy, CSS risks remaining dependent on project funding and partner goodwill. State actors need the resources to convene, review community evidence, act on findings and track commitments. Otherwise, community-led monitoring may continue to generate important evidence without a sufficiently resourced system to respond. Overall, these blind spots do not reduce the significance of CSS. They clarify what is required for the next phase: predictable payments, domestic budget lines, risk informed field operations, inflation-sensitive logistics, continuity planning with partners, faster government response and stronger state ownership. This is the shift needed for CSS to move from a successful project-supported accountability model to a sustained mechanism for PHC responsiveness, service quality and community trust. t: Descriptive Narrative The COVID-19 pandemic exposed
x: Descriptive Narrative The COVID-19 pandemic exposed significant vulnerabilities within Nigeria's health commodity supply chain. Prior to C19RM, fragmented warehousing systems, inadequate last-mile distribution, weak logistics visibility, limited performance monitoring of logistics service providers, inconsistent inventory management practices, and poor healthcare waste disposal systems constrained the country's ability to rapidly respond to public health emergencies. The project supported a series of strategic interventions aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s public health supply chain, improving accountability in commodity distribution, and advancing the transition toward an integrated and government-led supply chain system. The HPWM thematic area adopted an end-to-end supply chain approach covering forecasting, procurement, warehousing, distribution, and last-mile delivery. This component played a central role in ensuring the availability, quality assurance, and equitable access to essential diagnostics, case management tools, infection prevention supplies, and health system strengthening equipment.

t: Commodities were procured rapidly through multiple
x: Commodities were procured rapidly through multiple purchase orders between 2021 and 2022 using competent procurement mechanisms through WAMBO pooled procurement fund (GF preferred procurement platform) and diversified suppliers to respond to the rapidly evolving pandemic environment. The project strengthened a supply chain that had weaknesses at both ends, making it more capable and more visible through operational warehouses, logistics visibility and last-mile delivery. Rather than creating parallel COVID-19 logistics systems, the intervention deliberately strengthened existing national systems managed through the National Product Supply Chain Management Programme (NPSCMP), Federal Ministry of Health, National Agency for the Control of AIDS (NACA), disease programmes and state logistics structures. On the healthcare waste side, an initial plan to procure incinerators was redirected, after engagement with WHO, into a systems approach.

x: The interministerial healthcare-waste-management technical working group chaired by the Ministry of Environment and co-chaired by the Federal Ministry of Health was reactivated, a national assessment of facility waste handling across 12 states and the FCT was conducted and the findings informed the revised National Healthcare Waste Management Policy and Strategic Plan 2024 to 2028 and its costed implementation plan. In addition, the Global Fund, through its waste management service provider MEBS Global Reach, implemented the 2024 Expired/ Unusable Pharmaceutical and Laboratory Reagents Waste Drive across all 36 states and the FCT between July and November 2024. The exercise aimed to identify, retrieve, transport, and safely dispose of expired, damaged, and unusable. The HCWM component was primarily catalytic and policy-focused rather than commodity-intensive.

The Health Product Management, Supply Chain and Logistics intervention was designed to strengthen Nigeria's COVID-19 response through the procurement, distribution, management and sustainable use of essential health commodities. During the pandemic, the availability of diagnostics, PPE, laboratory supplies, oxygenrelated equipment and case-management tools became a critical determinant of response readiness, service continuity and facility-level preparedness. COVID-19 buttressed the fact that commodity availability depends on more than procurement. Products had to be forecasted, registered, purchased, quality-assured, warehoused, distributed, tracked, received at service-delivery points and safely managed after use. Weaknesses in any part of that chain could delay testing, interrupt infection-prevention measures, constrain case management or increase environmental and occupational risks from infectious healthcare waste.

t: QUALITY IMPROVEMENT DESCRIPTIVE NARRATIVE The Quality
x: QUALITY IMPROVEMENT DESCRIPTIVE NARRATIVE The Quality Improvement (QI) pillar was implemented as a strategic health systems strengthening intervention to improve the quality, safety, efficiency and continuity of healthcare services across supported facilities and communities in Nigeria. It responded to persistent quality-of-care gaps across HIV, Tuberculosis (TB), malaria, COVID-19, maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH) and broader primary healthcare (PHC) services. The 2018 Lancet Commission on High-Quality Health Systems in Low- and Middle-Income Countries found that clients receive less than half of the recommended evidence-based clinical actions during routine visits, and that poor-quality care now accounts for more deaths than the lack of access to care. This evidence framed the central premise of the pillar: that widening access alone is insufficient, and deliberate investment in the quality and effectiveness of care is required to translate access into better health outcomes.

It then provided more intensive support to selected states, LGAs and facilities based on epidemiological risk, service burden, existing gaps and the strategic importance of particular institutions. This approach reflected the realities of Nigeria’s federal health system. Public health threats require national standards, national coordination and systems that can exchange information across state boundaries. At the same time, detection, notification, verification, clinical care and community engagement occur within states, LGAs, facilities and communities.

The second was targeted support to states with identified gaps or higher implementation requirements. The third was investment in specialised institutions, including national and zonal laboratories, tertiary hospitals, emergency operations centres and training institutions whose functions extend beyond the state in which they are located. This differentiated pattern was not an inconsistency in programme delivery. It was a deliberate public health approach. National coverage established a minimum level of preparedness, while targeted and specialised investments strengthened areas that required greater depth or could provide services to a wider referral network. Only 155 health facilities, 26 laboratories, 25 points of entry and 15 treatment centres were directly connected to the system. Much of contact tracing and event documentation continued to depend on paper-based processes. C19RM expanded SORMAS into tertiary, secondary and selected primary health facilities across all 36 states and the FCT. The programme trained 5,084 users across more than 3,720 facilities and provided thousands of devices to support electronic reporting, case investigation, contact tracing and outbreak management.

t: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response training
x: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response training reached 40,437 health workers, clinicians, surveillance focal persons, laboratory personnel and Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers across 419 LGAs in 20 states that had not received the same level of support under earlier programmes. Reporting tools and standard guidance were distributed nationally. Programme results indicate a clear improvement in routine reporting. Completeness increased from 71 per cent to 93 per cent, while timeliness increased from 64 per cent to 85 per cent. The electronic IDSR platform generated 442,090 reports across 11 priority diseases. These improvements reflect the combined contribution of training, devices, supervision, standardised tools and stronger state and national coordination. They should not be attributed to any single intervention. C19RM also strengthened surveillance beyond routine facility reports.

t: Event-based surveillance was established or expanded
x: Event-based surveillance was established or expanded in 12 states, with 360 multisectoral participants trained to identify, assess and verify signals from media reports, hotlines, community sources and other informal channels. Community-based surveillance was piloted in Kano, Oyo and Enugu. Across 63 LGAs, 6,930 community informants, including community health workers, traditional leaders, volunteers and other trusted actors, were trained to report unusual illnesses, deaths, rumours and other events of potential public health importance. These investments created a more connected early-warning pathway. A signal identified in a community can be reported to an LGA surveillance officer, entered into SORMAS, verified by the state surveillance team, linked to laboratory testing and escalated through the State Public Health Emergency Operations Centre. The introduction of the 7-1-7 approach also provided a practical benchmark for assessing whether public health events are detected within seven days, notified within one day and responded to within seven days. 3.

t: The coordination system During the early
x: The coordination system During the early phase of the pandemic, the immediate priority was to protect health workers, expand testing, manage severe cases and prevent disruption to HIV, tuberculosis and malaria services. States required personal protective equipment, diagnostic materials, oxygen support, isolation capacity, infection prevention supplies and practical arrangements for maintaining access to essential care. As implementation progressed, C19RM moved beyond emergency distribution and increasingly focused on the systems required to use, coordinate and sustain the investments. The programme strengthened the structures required to use and manage the investments. These included state oxygen desks, laboratory quality systems, digital surveillance platforms, Public Health Emergency Operations Centres, community monitoring structures, pharmaceutical warehouses, health information systems and technical teams responsible for maintenance, reporting and supervision. The final phase placed greater emphasis on institutionalisation and sustainability. The main question was no longer only whether equipment had been procured or whether training had been conducted.

t: It was whether the systems were
x: It was whether the systems were functioning routinely, whether trained personnel remained available, whether information was being used for public health action, and whether government financing was available for power, connectivity, maintenance, reagents, supervision and emergency coordination. The State Technical Assistant model supported this process by maintaining a direct connection between national grant arrangements and state implementation. Technical Assistants followed delivery, supported coordination, escalated bottlenecks and worked with state institutions to translate national workplans into local action. This was particularly important in a programme delivered across 37 jurisdictions with different levels of infrastructure, staffing and financial capacity. As implementation progressed, C19RM moved beyond emergency distribution and increasingly focused on the systems required to use, coordinate and sustain the investments. t: technology, but it does require a
x: technology, but it does require a reliable system for collecting, transporting, tracking and reporting specimens and results. Taken together, these investments strengthened a tiered diagnostic network that supports routine disease programmes while also providing the confirmation capacity required for future outbreak response. The next priorities are to ensure reagent availability, complete the operationalisation of the zonal laboratories, sustain quality management and maintain equipment through functional biomedical engineering systems. Surveillance can only support effective public health action when signals are linked to timely laboratory confirmation. C19RM therefore strengthened diagnostic services across the national laboratory network, from peripheral testing sites to state, zonal and national reference laboratories. The GeneXpert optimisation project strengthened 396 laboratories across all states and the FCT. The support addressed the operating conditions required for reliable molecular testing, including solar power, inverters and batteries, air conditioning, cold-chain equipment, grounding, lightning protection and surge protection.

t: Personnel in 72 newly established GeneXpert
x: Personnel in 72 newly established GeneXpert sites received training and mentorship, while cartridge procurement and national distribution supported continuity of tuberculosis and drug-resistant tuberculosis testing. A further 333 Truenat platforms expanded molecular diagnosis across primary, secondary and tertiary levels. The equipment was selected in part because it can operate under difficult environmental conditions and can extend testing closer to populations that may not have easy access to central laboratories. Three hundred and seventy portable digital X-ray units strengthened tuberculosis screening and respiratory assessment in priority facilities. The electronic National Laboratory Information System was extended across the 774 LGAs, providing a foundation for test ordering, specimen tracking, result reporting and laboratory performance monitoring. The value of this system will depend on continued user support, data quality, connectivity and integration with surveillance and routine health information systems.

t: Six integrated zonal reference laboratories were
x: Six integrated zonal reference laboratories were established or strengthened at Federal Teaching Hospital Gombe, Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital, Jos University Teaching Hospital, University College Hospital Ibadan, Federal Teaching Hospital Owerri and University of Port Harcourt Teaching Hospital. These laboratories were designed to support HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, COVID-19 and other diseases of public health importance within a shared reference network. At national level, genomic surveillance was strengthened at the National Reference Laboratory in Gaduwa and the Central Public Health Laboratory in Lagos. A National Genomic Surveillance Strategy and national consortium provided a framework for sequencing and interpreting pathogens of public health importance, including COVID-19, Lassa fever, mpox and antimicrobial-resistant organisms. Quality management support reached 66 laboratories, including 56 tertiary laboratories and 10 Lagos State laboratories. A higher-performing group of 10 laboratories across Lagos, Oyo, Sokoto, Kaduna and Anambra received more intensive support toward ISO 15189 accreditation.

t: These laboratories should be described as
x: These laboratories should be described as progressing toward accreditation, pending completion of the relevant external assessments. Specimen referral pilots in Abia and Taraba used the Nigerian Postal Service to test a government-led approach for transporting specimens between peripheral and reference laboratories. This was an important public health lesson. Access to advanced testing does not require every facility to own every Expanding Laboratory Diagnosis and Confirmation

t: Medical oxygen became one of the
x: Medical oxygen became one of the most visible tests of hospital preparedness during COVID-19. C19RM strengthened a national oxygen platform comprising 73 pressure swing adsorption plants, including 63 procured through WAMBO and 10 procured locally. The plants were distributed across all states and the FCT. Most states received two plants, Adamawa received three, while Benue and Niger received one each. Twelve liquid oxygen tanks strengthened bulk storage in tertiary hospitals, and bedside oxygen piping was installed in 44 tertiary facilities across all states and the FCT. The FCT received installations in three facilities, while Bauchi, Benue, Edo, Jigawa and Lagos each had two supported tertiary facilities. Every other state had one facility included in the piping programme. The wider oxygen package included 21,291 cylinders, 2,086 ten-litre concentrators with power backup, 7,730 pulse oximeters, 690 oxygen analysers, 2,614 regulators, more than 30,000 flowmeters and more than 10,000 humidifiers.

t: These inputs strengthened oxygen production, storage,
x: These inputs strengthened oxygen production, storage, distribution, measurement and bedside administration. Clinical training reached 1,660 health workers across the federation. Average knowledge scores increased from 47 per cent before training to 73 per cent after training. Biomedical engineering training developed a national group of trainers and facility-based engineers responsible for preventive maintenance and repair. Across the wider oxygen programme, close to 700 biomedical engineers and technicians received training. State oxygen desks were established to coordinate planning, equipment tracking, functionality and sustainability. This created a formal state responsibility for oxygen services and made oxygen more visible within state health planning. Post-installation assessment showed that much of the infrastructure was functioning, but it also identified maintenance risks. Around four in five PSA plants assessed were operational, approximately nine in ten liquid oxygen tanks were in service and around 91 per cent of concentrators were functional.

t: Pulse oximeters showed lower functionality, partly
x: Pulse oximeters showed lower functionality, partly because of battery and charging problems. These findings are important for the next phase of oxygen system strengthening. The future of the oxygen investment will be determined not by the number of plants installed, but by plant uptime, oxygen purity, availability of power, maintenance response, cylinder movement and whether patients with hypoxaemia receive oxygen when it is required. Strengthening Medical Oxygen and Clinical Readiness Infection prevention and control became a central part of Nigeria’s pandemic response because it affected health worker protection, patient safety and continuity of routine services. C19RM supported a broad IPC network of 566 facilities across the country, while the dedicated systems-strengthening intervention worked more intensively with 171 secondary and tertiary facilities. All states and the FCT appointed and trained IPC focal persons and completed state-level IPC baseline assessments.

t: Six states, Borno, Cross River, Enugu,
x: Six states, Borno, Cross River, Enugu, FCT, Katsina and Ogun, received intensive assistance. Sixteen states developed IPC strategic plans, exceeding the initial target of six states. A national REDCap platform was established for IPC assessment and surveillance. It brought together state and facility assessment tools, hand-hygiene readiness measures, scorecards and healthcare-associated infection surveillance forms. The platform created a basis for national reporting, although the next step is to ensure that facilities and states receive timely feedback and use the information for improvement. A complementary PHC revitalisation investment upgraded 157 primary health centres across 28 states and 139 LGAs. This addressed the physical requirements for safer care, including facility infrastructure, water, sanitation, equipment and spaces needed for triage and infection prevention. The first national healthcare-associated infection point prevalence survey was conducted in six sentinel facilities, one in each geopolitical zone.

t: The survey included 1,177 patients across
x: The survey included 1,177 patients across 107 wards and found a pooled HAI prevalence of 3.7 per cent. Antimicrobial use was recorded in 71 per cent of patients. Surgical site infections were the most common HAI, followed by pneumonia, urinary tract infection and bloodstream infection. The survey provided an important baseline for patient safety, antimicrobial stewardship and antimicrobial resistance. It should become the beginning of routine surveillance and improvement, rather than remain a one-time exercise. Infection Prevention, Patient Safety and Safer Health Facilities

t: The pandemic affected access to HIV,
x: The pandemic affected access to HIV, tuberculosis and malaria services through movement restrictions, reduced facility attendance, pressure on health workers and disruption to laboratory and commodity systems. C19RM therefore supported service-continuity measures in addition to the direct COVID-19 response. The core HIV continuity package operated in 13 states: Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Edo, Enugu, Gombe, Imo, Kaduna, Kano, Kwara, Oyo, Plateau and Taraba. The package included community delivery, multi-month dispensing, home delivery, community pharmacies, virtual case management, telemedicine and digital programme coordination. More focused interventions supported decentralised community viral load and early infant diagnosis in Anambra and Ebonyi, and COVID-19 screening and vaccination support for people living with HIV in Anambra, Abia, Ebonyi and Taraba. Tuberculosis mitigation had national reach through GeneXpert optimisation, training, cartridge procurement and distribution. Malaria mitigation supported COVID-safe surveys and campaigns, digital field tools and ICT4D systems.

t: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention reached more than
x: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention reached more than six million children across eight states, while 652 personnel received training in digital campaign tools. The experience confirmed that preparedness also includes the ability to maintain essential health services during a public health emergency. Community delivery, longer medication refills, resilient diagnostics and digital coordination should therefore remain part of routine disease-programme planning. Twenty-two pharmaceutical-grade warehouse sites were established or upgraded across 21 states, with the Abuja Premier Medical Warehouse serving the federal platform. Lagos had two warehouse sites, reflecting the volume of commodities managed within the state. Integrated last-mile distribution was piloted in Yobe and Nasarawa. National logistics information systems, product traceability and fourth-party logistics arrangements strengthened commodity visibility and distribution. Healthcare waste management combined targeted assessments with a national retrieval and disposal exercise. Health information support was also differentiated.

t: Data-quality assessment capacity was strengthened in
x: Data-quality assessment capacity was strengthened in 23 states, analytics training reached 132 LGAs in six states, and 2,524 facility staff in Borno, Cross River, Nasarawa, Kogi and Enugu received support on NHMIS tools. Reporting in the supported settings improved from below 40 per cent to around 90 per cent. Quality improvement was concentrated in Ekiti, Gombe and Jigawa. Direct C19RM support reached 504 facilities across all 44 LGAs in the three states. State-financed expansion added 317 facilities, bringing the total to 821. This was one of the clearest examples of a state government extending a grant-supported intervention through domestic resources. Protecting HIV, Tuberculosis and Malaria Services Supply Chain, Health Information and Quality Improvement Public health response depends on trust, timely information and an understanding of how communities perceive risk.

t: C19RM strengthened national messaging while also
x: C19RM strengthened national messaging while also supporting states to collect and use information on public concerns, misinformation, service access and trusted sources of health information. Risk communication capacity and needs assessments were conducted in 12 states using 120 key informant interviews and 48 focus group discussions. The process involved health educators, epidemiologists, surveillance officers, traditional and religious leaders, media organisations, community actors and government information structures. Community perception polling collected more than 20,000 responses across 20 states and 40 LGAs. Two hundred trained field workers collected 1,000 responses per state, generating locally relevant information on cholera, Lassa fever and other priority public health threats. Dashboards enabled state teams to review findings and adjust messages to respond to local concerns. More than 500 cholera community-engagement guides were distributed across 22 states.

t: NCDC-supported digital content, including the Health
x: NCDC-supported digital content, including the Health Tori radio drama series, reached more than 200,000 people through online platforms, in addition to broadcast audiences. The public health value of this work extended beyond the number of messages disseminated. It provided states with a structured way to understand what communities believed, which rumours were circulating, what information sources were trusted and what barriers might prevent people from following public health advice or seeking care. C19RM strengthened national messaging while also supporting states to collect and use information on public concerns, misinformation, service access and trusted sources of health information. t: Lagos occupied a distinct position within
x: Lagos occupied a distinct position within the C19RM response. Nigeria’s first confirmed COVID-19 case was recorded in the state on 27 February 2020, and Lagos rapidly became the centre of the early national response. The state also experienced disruption to routine services, including an estimated 13 per cent decline in tuberculosis notifications during the early period of the pandemic. Unlike other states, Lagos managed a dedicated C19RM envelope of US$5.44 million as a subnational Principal Recipient. This gave the Lagos State Ministry of Health direct responsibility for procurement, distribution, implementation and reporting through its established grant-management and public financial-management structures. The investment approach in Lagos focused on depth and specialised national functions. Lagos was not included in every broad state-coverage intervention. It was outside the 28-state PHC revitalisation programme, the 13-state core HIV continuity package and the 20-state IDSR training package.

t: These were targeted primarily at states
x: These were targeted primarily at states with different baseline needs. In Lagos, the priority was to strengthen advanced laboratory, biosecurity, emergency-care and supply-chain functions. C19RM supported the biosafety level 3 laboratory node at the Mainland Hospital and Infectious Disease Hospital complex in Yaba. The investment included real-time PCR equipment, scientific freezers, laboratory commodities and digital specimen-tracking equipment such as laptops, tablets, barcode scanners and QR systems. Ten Lagos State laboratories received quality-management support, and six of the 10 laboratories selected nationally for intensive ISO 15189 readiness support were located in Lagos. These included General Hospital Lagos, Mainland Hospital, Lagos Island Maternity Hospital, the NIMR Tuberculosis Reference Laboratory, General Hospital Isolo and General Hospital Onikan. The laboratories were supported toward accreditation and should not be described as accredited pending external assessment. Lagos also hosted national genomic sequencing functions and the upgraded Central Public Health Laboratory.

t: These investments support pathogen detection, outbreak
x: These investments support pathogen detection, outbreak investigation and national surveillance beyond the boundaries of the state. The state received two PSA plants, one liquid oxygen tank at Lagos University Teaching Hospital and bedside oxygen piping in two tertiary facilities. The Lagos University Teaching Hospital School of Biomedical Engineering also served as a national training centre for engineers and technicians involved in oxygen maintenance. Emergency case management was strengthened through eight mobile intensive care ambulances under the Lagos State Ambulance Service. The state subsequently financed fuel, preventive maintenance and insurance, providing evidence that the service had moved into routine state operations. Isolation and treatment centres, including Onikan and Gbagada, received beds, protective equipment and clinical supplies. Lagos was the only state with two pharmaceutical-grade warehouse sites.

t: A documented distribution cycle reached more
x: A documented distribution cycle reached more than 80 facilities, including teaching hospitals, general hospitals and primary health centres across LGAs such as Agege, Ajeromi-Ifelodun, Alimosho, Amuwo-Odofin, Eti-Osa and Kosofe. Lagos State: From Pandemic Epicentre to National Public Health Anchor Community-led monitoring operated through 15 CBOs, while risk communication needs assessments supported more localised public engagement. Lagos also served as one of three hubs for the IPC diploma programme. The Lagos experience indicates that direct state responsibility can support faster implementation and clearer ownership where grant management, technical leadership and public financial systems are sufficiently established. The model cannot be transferred automatically to every state, but it demonstrates the value of aligning financing, decision-making and responsibility within the institution expected to sustain the investment. Lagos also shows why specialised investments in one state can serve the wider country.

t: Genomic sequencing, high-containment laboratories, quality-assured reference
x: Genomic sequencing, high-containment laboratories, quality-assured reference services, biomedical engineering training and emergency referral systems provide national as well as state-level value. Lessons Learned • C19RM established a national platform, but national coverage does not by itself mean that every supported system is functioning at the same level. States differ in staffing, infrastructure, recurrent financing, supervision, maintenance and the extent to which new responsibilities have been integrated into routine government systems. The first priority is to establish one validated national register of C19RM-supported sites and investments. The register should show what was procured, where it was delivered, whether it was installed and commissioned, whether it is currently functional, who owns it and what is required to sustain it. • The second priority is to track functionality rather than presence alone. Oxygen monitoring should include uptime, purity, downtime and patient access.

t: Laboratory monitoring should include test volumes,
x: Laboratory monitoring should include test volumes, turnaround time, reagent availability and quality performance. Surveillance monitoring should include reporting quality, signal verification and public health action. PHEOC monitoring should include staffing, activation, exercises and documented use during actual events. The third priority is to sustain recurrent costs. Electricity, data connectivity, laboratory reagents, maintenance, software hosting, supervision, community transport and emergency exercises are central to preparedness and response. They should be included in federal and state budgets rather than treated as temporary project costs. The fourth priority is to retain and update the workforce. Surveillance officers, biomedical engineers, laboratory personnel, IPC focal persons, emergency managers, data staff and community actors require continuing training, supervision and clear institutional roles. • The fifth priority is to maintain community trust and feedback.

t: Community-based surveillance, community-led monitoring and risk
x: Community-based surveillance, community-led monitoring and risk communication should be connected to formal state and national processes so that signals and concerns are acknowledged, verified and acted upon. The central public health lesson is that preparedness is built between emergencies. C19RM strengthened the systems through which Nigeria detects public health threats, confirms them, coordinates response, provides clinical care and protects essential services. Sustaining these systems will depend on state ownership, routine use, domestic financing and continued national coordination.

The asset-density lens, and how to read it The value of the lens is to help identify where functionality, ownership, maintenance and routine use should be reviewed next.

t: The honest reading of the subnational
x: The honest reading of the subnational map is a tension between universality and depth. C19RM achieved something close to universal coverage -almost every state shows a broad asset array - but coverage and capability are not the same, and depth varies sharply with state institutional capacity, workforce, financing and maintenance readiness. The strategic implication is that the next phase should not be designed around a flat "36 states and the FCT" narrative. It should be differentiated by what each state can now do. That argues for sorting states into three broad groups for the transition. High-density, high-capacity states can serve as demonstration hubs for integrated preparedness - oxygen sustainability, digital dashboards, IPC maturity, laboratory-network functionality. Moderate-density states need targeted technical support, functionality checks and maintenance planning. Lower-density or weakly documented states need readiness diagnostics, data validation and institutional-absorption support before anything else.

t: A state preparedness-maturity scorecard -classifying states
x: A state preparedness-maturity scorecard -classifying states by ownership, functionality, workforce, data use, financing and maintenance readiness - would turn this map from a description into a planning instrument. The subnational map is the portfolio's clearest argument that preparedness is decided locally. National coverage created the footprint; state absorption will decide whether the footprint becomes capability. The immediate task is to validate the register - confirming site locations, functionality, ownership and recurrent-cost arrangements - and then to use it, through a maturity scorecard and differentiated transition support, so that strong states consolidate and thinner states are helped to catch up rather than fall behind. The geographic narrative and the sustainability narrative are the same narrative seen from different angles, and both point to the forward agenda the next chapter sets out. 7. t: From emergency financing to institutional capacity
x: From emergency financing to institutional capacity C19RM's strategic value in Nigeria lies in how emergency financing was used to strengthen the response, protect essential programmes and build institutional capacity for the public-health threats still to come. It was never only a COVID-19 grant. Across all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, it became a national implementation mechanism — translating roughly US$336.2 million of realised investment, within an approved envelope of about US$401.6 million, into a financed response, protected HIV, tuberculosis and malaria services, and a widening base of pandemic-preparedness systems. The investment entered the health system at a moment of real uncertainty, when the country had to act quickly while holding on to accountability, continuity of care and public trust.

t: Over time its centre of gravity
x: Over time its centre of gravity shifted from acute response toward stronger public-health functions: surveillance, laboratories, medical oxygen, infection prevention and control, health products and waste management, the workforce, community systems and data systems. That movement mirrors the wider Global Fund shift from COVID-19 control toward resilient and sustainable systems for health. For Nigeria, the value is not simply that money was mobilised; it is that the money reached institutions, states, facilities, laboratories, communities and service platforms in ways that now leave a stronger basis for the next response. Strengthening the response through Nigerian institutions The portfolio worked because it moved through Nigerian institutions rather than around them.

t: NACA, NTBLCP and the Lagos State
x: NACA, NTBLCP and the Lagos State Ministry of Health held Principal Recipient roles, while the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control, Federal Ministry of Health departments, NMEP, NASCP, NPHCDA, NPSCMP, the State Ministries of Health, civil-society networks, technical partners and facility teams turned financing into delivery. This institutional route matters. Preparedness cannot be sustained by temporary project structures; it has to sit inside the public-health institutions responsible for surveillance, diagnostics, emergency coordination, clinical readiness, health products, community engagement and service continuity. C19RM strengthened those routes, even where the process was hard, and it showed where the system still needs work: faster fund flow, clearer implementation roles, stronger state absorption, better asset visibility and more deliberate recurrent financing. These are not back-office details. They are the conditions that decide whether emergency investments become lasting capacity.

t: Systems value across the response chain

Medical oxygen was scarce in many settings. Laboratory capacity remained concentrated and distant from many points of patient presentation. Supply chains were under stress.
